responses.mission_1.search: On the open map, the BFS and A* path lengths provided are both 13.5 and expanded-node counts for BFS is 928 and A* is 700. A* examined fewer cells. Both BFS and A* algorithms return the shortest route so the equal path is expected but with the cells they expand there's a slight difference. BFS expands a bit larger than A* because with BFS it expands all around the start counting all its neighbors cells initially then all of the neighbors neighbors and so on, It doesn't know where the goal is so it explores everything evenly like a ripple. popleft() takes out the cell that has been waiting the longest and every new cell that gets appended goes to the back so this just opens all the cells closest to the start first and it'll know the goal has been found whenever the goal itself gets popped. As for A* it uses a heap ordered with heuristics so when it  pops a new cell it updates g and h which indicate the steps taken and the distance left to the goal, if the algorithm see's it's getting closer to the goal it will continue that way, if it see's that it get's further away from the goal then it may not expand that path as there's a shorter heuristic somewhere else. This is the reason why there's fewer expansions, BFS explores all around from the start until it reaches the goal like a ripple, While A* is also a ripple however it's weighted more towards the goal section because it know's where the goal is.
responses.mission_1.failure: The DFS and IDDFS rows covers basically 3x (visually) the amount that the BFS covers on the constrained map,  for expansions DFS is 524, 250001 for IDDFS ,848 for BFS. IDDFS expands 250001 nodes because it does not keep track of the globally visited nodes and explores every path up to it's depth limit over and over again, basically cells can be revisited multiple times so the expansions increase exponentially, For DFS it just explores all the way down a branch until it reaches the goal so the expansion would be way less as it's not looking at everything but it can still take a longer path as it could be exploring a lot of unnecessary cells. BFS once again just explores all neighboring cells around the start and ripples out from that but this one does grab shortest path. For the 4 unreachable-case statuses they basically all could not find a valid path because the S was enclosed in one room and the G was enclosed in another with no valid pathing. The difference between no_path and resource_limit is no_path means that the search was completed but no goal could be found meaning that it was unreachable, whereas resource_limit means the algorithm was stopped before it finished whether it took too long or ran out of expansion budget so it never reached a goal but does not necessarily mean that the goal was unreachable or that there was no goal. Claude was used to help with starting pathing code especially with IDDFS as it was the most confusing however checked that the proper data structures were used and specific cases for each algorithm like iddfs not keeping a global visited, astar stopping when goal is popped.
responses.mission_2.prediction: Nav2 Smac 2D and A*, if Nav2 is a cost-aware A* with smoothing then it should finish slightly sooner than A* since they both provide a cost based bath but Nav2 has smoothing.
responses.mission_2.performance: Looking at A* and Nav2 for the constrained map, both of their statuses for successful, elapsed_s for A* was 90.358, for Nav2 it was 73.698, Distance_m for A* was 23.8191 and Distance_m for Nav2 was 20.5792. This result does support my prediction that Nav2 would be slightly faster because the distance covered is a lot less and the elapsed time was nearly 20 seconds faster. The reasoning for this is the turns that Nav2 takes, it seems to be taking a sort of euclidean distance for determing how to move compared to A* which used manhattan distance causing it to take just slightly longer.
responses.mission_2.choice: Not sure what this question is asking, Nav2 should be chosen simply cause it's just a slightly better A*, they both have success status and Nav2 will always have slightly faster execution time. Distance for Nav2 will usually always be better simply cause it's using euclidean distancing instead of manhattan, speed and precision would be the most important so with the tracking error being super low where it's still generally on the line is nice and how long it takes.
responses.mission_3.prediction: Changing the repulsion strength from 0 to 1.30 changed how far the robot moved away from the robot turned away from the person before oscillating back to its original path, mainly looking at the constrained map but at 0 it was just a straight line no turns at all just regular path, at 1.30 it started to create these small little bumps. Changing the influence distance also determines if the robots needs to actually bounce at all or if it can just go straight ahead.
responses.mission_3.comparison: The completed condition with the largest minimum_person_clearance_m for rrt  was social_1 with 1.7268. compared to it's baseline it was a very minor change with a 0.0001 increase, the person_space_s value stayed the same amongst both.  As for A* highest minimum_person_clearance_m was social_2 with 0.7719. compared to it's baseline the value increases and the personal_space_s value dropped from 1.8 to 0.  Having wider spacing did not cost more time nor distance with rrt just being faster in general as well as traveling a shorter distance while still maintaining a wide enough space away from the person.
responses.mission_3.recommendation: Rrt should be the planner, status succeeded, condition can be either baseline or social_1 depending if saving a bit of time and distance is worth the 0.0001 clearance. Static-person trials do not show the possibilities of needing to reroute or stop if there were moving people an example being if a robot creates a path based on where humans are initially but then a human later walks into the robots path and stops there, now there's an issue of deciding whether continue waiting or creating another path.
responses.final.synthesis: A route is suitable for a robot sharing space with people if it can balance efficiency, navigation accuracy, and safety for the people within the environment. Just because a robot is fast or slow does not mean it's a good robot, it needs to be able to avoid obstacles, not take any unnecessary detours and evaluate a proper route algorithm that does not put pedestrians at risk or make them feel uncomfortable. Shorter routes may sound nice but could pass really close to people or obstacles, a longer route may sound worse but could be the safest as it doesn't take sharp turns and ensures that it stays predictable. To also search effectively and not explore unnecessarily and find a good route.  Route quality, some path's may look good but is there a better one that isn't exploring unnecessary routes or doing random backtracking over and over again. Being able to avoid objects on a map and detect if a route is even possible in the first place based on a map or if there were moving humans, can it maintain reasonable spacing to ensure safety, can it adjust its directions if a pedestrian is suddenly in front of them without causing harm and still remaining predictable. Having all these conditions is what makes a route good for a robot, it need's to be somewhat efficient but it cannot trade safety for efficiency.
responses.final.course_reflection: This activity was probably one of the best activities yet, I enjoyed being able to code up the different algorithms and seeing them work, the questions that were being asked were also mostly pretty explanatory,  I didn't struggle to understand what some things meant and could answer most questions. Towards the end the questions slowly started to get a bit more confusing when it became more general but it was still fine. Overall I enjoyed this activity and would continue to do this in the future.
